newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Bitter UK election may be won by party accountants.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bitter UK election may be won by party accountants.

text.p: Britain's politicians have ended their summer breaks and unsheathed their knives ahead of an election no more than eight months away and set to be the most bitterly fought in recent history.

But even as strategists and spin-doctors -- transformed by the press in recent months from shadowy figures to media stars in their own right -- plot their next moves, it is the party accountants who are working hardest behind the scenes.
Just like the fight for the support of voters, shown by opinion polls to be overwhelmingly behind Labour, the opposition appears to be winning the battle for the cheque book.

Labour leader Tony Blair's decision to ditch the party's socialist dogmas and woo business leaders, dubbed by the press the "prawn cocktail offensive" in reference to the constant round of City of London lunches, is literally paying off.

Labour crowned a conference for Britain's top businessmen on September 4 with a ringing endorsement of Blair by Cob Stenham, chairman of Anglo-French packaging group Arjo Wiggins, the first head of a top British-listed company to publicly back Labour.

Just a day later came the first financial fruits when insurance boss Matthew Harding, co-owner of Prime Minister John Major's favourite soccer team, Chelsea, gave Labour one million pounds ($1.57 million).
Labour said it had received donations in 1995 which had helped it to build a campaign "war chest" of 4.4 million pounds.

With a new and aggressive telephone fund-raising campaign and receipts from a flood of new members, Labour -- 20 to 30 points ahead in polls even after a recent Conservative fightback -- is confident of more than doubling that by the election.
The contrast with the Conservatives could not be starker.
As Labour's bank balance has swelled, the ruling party has had to scramble to cover huge bank debts left mainly from its victorious 1992 election campaign.

At the same time, corporate donorsm, under pressure from shareholders to boost profits, have cut back on donations to the party which has held a stranglehold on power for 17 years but which many feel is now destined for a spell in opposition.

Key backers like the engineering group Lucas Industries, car distributor Inchcape, drinks firms Allied Domecq and Whitbread, British Airways and even United Biscuits, for many years the party's biggest supporter, have stopped donations.
Earlier this year, aero-engine maker Rolls-Royce, which was privatised by the government in 1987, disclosed in its annual report that it had paid nothing to the Conservatives last year.
The move surprised the City, which pointed to the importance of political contacts for Rolls-Royce's defence-related business, but it showed the way the wind is blowing.

A survey by Labour Research, a magazine funded by trade unions and recognised as a leading monitor of political funding, has estimated more than 100 companies deserted the Conservatives since 1992, slashing corporate donations by a third.
Conservative fundraisers shrug this off, saying last month that a surge in donations had allowed the party to pay off a bank overdraft which stood at 11.4 million pounds in March 1995.
But analysts say the party has only managed this by taking interest-free loans totalling over eight million pounds from local party associations, companies and rich supporters.
Labour has been making political capital out of the fact the Conservatives -- already under fire after a series of sleaze scandals -- refuse to say where their money comes from.
Companies are required by law to reveal political donations in their annual reports. Private donations are unregulated.
Labour has seized on disclosures that Asil Nadir, former chief of the Polly Peck group which crashed with multi-million pound debts, gave the Conservatives 400,000 pounds.

Nadir is now a fugitive from British justice in the Turkish part of Cyprus, but the Conservatives have returned none of the money, a clear sign, according to Labour, that the funding system needs reform.
The amounts involved are tiny compared to the United States.

There, the federal government limits spending by a candidate in the presidential primaries and the election to just under $100 million, although the sky is the limit if a contender decides not to accept federal funds.
In contrast, election spending limits on British candidates for parliament are among the world's strictest -- around 8,000 pounds each.

Spending by parties on advertising and other activities is unlimited and a 1994 study by the left-wing IPPR think-tank showed the Conservatives spent just 11.2 million pounds in their 1992 general election campaign.
With the bill for new poster campaigns in August alone estimated at around 900,000 pounds each for Labour and the Conservatives, the key is still spending power.
The IPPR study showed Conservatives have outspent Labour at every election for which figures are available.
But in 1992, the difference fell to just five percent when Labour spent 10.6 million pounds, slashing the Conservative majority to 21 from over 100 seats five years earlier.
With its funds still growing, Labour believes the advantage in the battle of the balance sheets may finally be moving its way, bringing an election victory even closer. ($1=.6373 Pound)
